newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's leaders mourn dead in rebel Kurd conflict.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's leaders mourn dead in rebel Kurd conflict.

text.p: Turkish political and army leaders led mourning on Thursday for soldiers who died on a cross-border mission in a helicopter crash that brought home the state's 13-year-old conflict with rebel Kurds.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, President Suleyman Demirel, ministers and military chiefs looked on sombrely at an Ankara mosque as prayers were said over the 11 soldiers' coffins, each draped in Turkey's star-and-crescent flag.

"These marytrs have given their lives and become a part of the motherland," the country's leading religious figure, Mehmet Nuri Yilmaz, told several thousand mourners gathered in the driving rain in the courtyard of the city's largest mosque.
More than 24,000 have died in fighting between the security forces and the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), who seek autonomy or independence in the mainly Kurdish southeast of Turkey.

Some mourners had pinned to their lapels pictures of the 11 dead, eight of them officers and two of them high-ranking, who were killed when their Cougar troop carrier went down in Iraq's mountainous Zap region on Wednesday.
The crowd sang the national anthem and some chanted anti-PKK slogans as an honour guard carried out the coffins, followed by grieving relatives.

"I am the wife of a soldier, I cannot cry. I do not want to give the scum the pleasure. I will make my son a soldier," Sadiye Guvercin, the wife of one of the deceased, was quoted as saying by Anatolian news agency.
Armed forces chief General Ismail Hakki Karadayi cut short a visit to Paris for the ceremony, attended mostly by forces personnel and broadcast live on several television channels.

The soldiers were on a mission in pursuit of PKK guerrillas as part of a three-week-old incursion into northern Iraq. At least 10,000 Turkish troops, backed by air power, have been in the region since May 14 in search of the rebels who use it as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
Turkish forces killed 14 Kurdish rebels and one soldier died in a clash in the eastern Turkish province of Erzincan, Anatolian said on Thursday.
The cause of Wednesday's helicopter crash remained unclear and was still being investigated after earlier reports of a technical failure, according to television channels.

A spokesman for the pro-Kurdish television channel Med TV said PKK guerrillas brought down a helicopter with a missile during fighting in the Zap region. The helicopter was hit as it was ferrying officers off Sikifta-Birindera mountain as a rebel attack drew close to over-running the peak, he said.
Iraqi opposition sources say the rebels shot down two Turkish helicopters earlier in the operation.
Ankara has previously acknowleged the loss of one chopper because of what it says was a technical fault.

The incursion has attracted condemnation from the Arab League secretariat and a demand that Turkish forces withdraw immediately. Some of NATO-member Turkey's Western allies and the United Nations secretary-general have criticised the operation.
Turkey says its forces have killed more than 2,000 rebels so far, but it has not given regular figures for government losses.
The rebels say they have killed 791 men from the opposite side -- Turkish soldiers, their allies in a "village guard" militia and guerrillas of Iraq's Kurdistan Democratic Party.
The operation has been conducted under a news blackout, making independent confirmation of reports impossible.
